      "original": "### 1. Gulliver Dornal\nGulliver Dornal, Male Human Exp9: CR 8; Medium Humanoid ; hp 35; Fort +4, Ref +2, Will +7;\n\n## STR 16, DEX 9, CON 13, INT 12, WIS 13, CHA 11.\n\nSkills: Appraise +10, Craft (Blacksmithing) +11, Craft (Carpentry) +8, Craft (Leatherworking) +6, Craft (Locksmithing) +10.\n\n## Trading Post\n\n### Role in the Campaign\n\nIn most fantasy campaigns, much of the adventure takes places beyond the borders of the so-called civilized lands. While adventures do occur in more urban settings, the traditional quests for lost tombs and lairs of vile beasts still tend to be set in wilder, less settled areas.\n\nIn many cases, the remoteness of the location will pose something of a problem to adventurers in search of supplies. Small homesteads or mining camps will rarely have the kind of gear sought after by professional adventurers, and more importantly will not be interested in purchasing or trading for the various trinkets and baubles that adventurers might haul out of the depths of some dank tomb. Into this void comes the trading post.\n\nMuch like the general store in a larger urban setting, the trading post is a multi- purpose business. Often these businesses are part store, part tavern, part post-office, and part community center. For those hardy souls who spend their lives on the frontier, a trip to the trading post is often a much anticipated break from the routine of their lives. Generations of locals likely have met weekly at the local post, exchanged news, griped about the weather, or taxes, or marauding trolls, and sneered at itinerant adventurers.\n\nWhen adventurers first arrive in a new rural locale, it behooves them to seek out a reliable source for equipment, and trading posts are generally good places to obtain hard to find items. Chances are, if the post doesn’t have a mundane bit of adventuring gear, it can get it – though delivery of the item may take time.\n\nThe hardy souls who set off to open trading posts in the more remote corners of the world are not shy, diffident storekeepers. They are often former adventurers themselves who enjoy the steady contact with members of their former profession. Regardless of their past experience, they are almost invariably tough individualists who are willing and capable of defending their small business. Given the nature of most campaign worlds, trading posts will tend to be easily defensible, fortified places.\n\n## Variations on the theme\n\nContrary to the norm, a naïve, sickly-looking young man and his beautiful young bride run the trading post the party has arrived at. They have come to the frontier in search of a new life and haven’t the slightest idea of the dangers they face. They are still unpacking their wagon when the party first arrives, and honorable adventurers will be hard pressed to leave these newcomers to their obvious fate…\n\nThe party may stumble upon a trading post which offers bounties on the heads of various local nuisance humanoids or monsters. Goblins, orcs, trolls, and similar creatures are good candidates for bounties. The party may view this as “free” money, since they are likely to be routinely dispatching such foes anyway, but if the adventurers just happen to be at the trading post when the local monsters decide its time for some\n\npayback, a nasty battle could develop.\n\nTrading posts needn’t deal solely in the mundane. A wizard might well set up a trading post in a region where particularly rare or valuable magical components might be found, and do a brisk business trading mundane items and equipment for gems, herbs, flowers, insects, body parts, or other things with arcane potential.\n\n## Toll Road/Bridge\n\n## NOTE: The floorplan for this locale was done at a scale of 1 square = 10 feet – different than all the others!\n\n## Role in the Campaign\n\nThose who travel the roads and rivers of most fantasy worlds can readily attest to the truth of the old saying the nothing in this life is free. In particular, the use of roads and byways is rarely without costs. Whether those costs need be paid in coin or blood is not always clear.\n\nIn most cases those demanding tolls for the use of roads, bridges and fords, will be representatives of the legitimate ruler of the region. After all, it costs money to build, maintain, and patrol the roads, and surely those costs ought to be borne by those who benefit from the infrastructure. These tolls are rarely prohibitive as most local authorities have learned that given enough financial incentive, merchants and other travelers will find other ways to get to their destination. The trick is finding a toll that enriches the toll-taker without being inconvenient enough to drive business away.\n\nWhile individual tolls might not prove too much of a burden, in particularly populated areas they can become a nuisance. Areas in which control of the lands is particularly fragmented or subinfeudated may result in travelers being stopped every few miles to pay another toll. The financial costs will be unlikely to seriously inconvenience any but the most impoverished adventuring party, but heroes in a hurry may find the delays on busy roads to be maddening.\n\nIn more remote areas, away from any lawful force that might frown upon the\n\npractice, tolls may be collected by anyone with the arm strength to enforce them. Whether this be a band of woodland merry men or a powerful individual or monster, these tolls are often more painful than the legitimate type and are generally indistinguishable from outright theft.\n\nDMs should be creative in thinking about tolls. Not all treasures sought by the toll taker are monetary. A particularly nasty undead creature might Haunt a river ford where it drowned and demand to drain some lifeforce (or even an entire life) in exchange for passage. A mysterious knight might insist on a test of arms before anyone can cross the bridge. A leprechaun might expect an answer to a riddle.\n\n## Variations on the theme\n\nAn adventuring party on a particularly time sensitive quest may find an encounter with a particularly officious toll taker to be infuriating. Make sure the small, bumbling bureaucrat in charge of the station is backed up by the full weight of the local authorities (making it less likely that more chaotic characters will simply hack their way through). Invent any number of regulations that require special tolls or paperwork to drag out the encounter. “Oh, you’re a Half-Orc. Let me see, I think that requires Form H8… Yes, here it is… Oh my, there’s a different algorithmic table of tolls for Half-Orcs. Let me get my abacus…” To add insult to injury, insist in payment in an obscure local currency – exact change only.\n\nCharacters arriving at a toll station discover the station manager and all his attendants dead. As they are investigating the scene, a strong force of the King’s cavalry arrives and takes them for murdering bandits…\n\nA monastery of spiritually pure, but obnoxiously self-righteous monks have established a toll booth of sorts across a mountain pass that the party simply must get through. Not interested in monetary tolls, the monks insist that anyone passing through must agree to perform a service “for the good of all”. Creative parties might think up relatively impressive sounding, but not very taxing, services.\n\n## The Troll Bridge\n\n(Text to be read to players)\n\n_As the road winds towards the river, you can clearly see ahead of you a sturdy, three-span stone bridge. The water is high and running fast, no doubt from the recent rains, as the omnipresent dark clouds serve to remind you. A giant-sized cottage stands beside the bridge, smoke curling lazily from the chimney. In front of the house, a tidy, tended garden plot shows signs of careful attention. A faint whiff of baking bread stirs your senses, perhaps aided by the memory of the depressing number of travel rations you’ve recently consumed._\n\n_The bridge appears at first glance to be just like any other stone bridge you have seen recently; perhaps a little old and run-down, but apparently structurally sound and sturdy. What is different, at least for a bridge this far away from a town or even a village, is the large cottage standing at the near end of the bridge. Other than its unusual size – the door is some 10 feet tall_\n\n_-- It would not be out of place in a quiet country thorp, or outside the walls of a baronial manor, but here, unprotected by liege or law, it defies sense that such an unfortified structure should survive the depredations of predators._\n\n_At the side of the road a crudely lettered sign has been affixed to a post, sagging to one side as it dangles from the single nail: Troll Bridge._\n\n(End players’ text)\n\n## Overview\n\nBeyond the frontiers of the civilized world, in the wilderness where there is no law save what one can assert by force of arms, many are the creatures and forces that find novel ways to amass wealth. Some will naturally seek to enrich themselves through outright theft and/or violence, but some find other ways to part travelers from their coin, albeit often with a thinly veiled threat of that same violence. If nobles and merchants can turn bridges into tollbooths, why should not a Troll?\n\nAs the characters approach the Troll bridge, they will be confronted by a very odd Troll who will seek to charge them a toll to cross his bridge. The Troll is quite powerful, but has a strong distaste for physical confrontation. Although he will fight if cornered, he prefers to attempt to reason with travelers and, if necessary, will allow them to cross the bridge (at least part way). The center of the bridge is trapped, and the unwary could well find themselves bobbing in the river. Retrieving and looting drowned corpses is still easier than fighting to this Troll’s way of thinking.\n\nThe party has arrived at the only bridge for many miles across a deep, fast-running\n\nriver. Arturus, an unusual Troll, has claimed the bridge and makes a comfortable living exacting tolls from passers-by.\n\nThe bridge crosses a wide expanse of water, its three stone spans bearing the weight of the 250-foot long bridge. It is wide enough for one fully loaded wagon and sturdy and strong despite it looking a bit aged. It was built more than 150 years ago by dwarves, working on commission for a mage, the ruins of whose tower can be found about a mile down the road on the other side of the bridge. As most things built by and for wizards, the bridge has its own magical secret (see description of Arturus the Troll below).\n\nIt is built of mixed field-stones, and held together by marvelous dwarven engineering with nary a drop of mortar. It has clearly seen much use over the years as its smooth surface shows the ruts of much cart and wagon traffic. The roadway over the bridge is flanked on either side by a low stone wall, approximately three feet high, to prevent the careless or the inebriated from plunging unexpectedly into the water.\n\nThe river is currently up and running high due to recent rains, and there is a barely a five foot gap between the rushing current and the bottom of the bridge. The water roars angrily between the spans, swirling madly before calming once past the structure. The water is stirred up and murky, with much debris and not a few small tree trucks bobbing past the bridge.\n\n## Cottage Exterior\n\nThe cottage is clearly built for giant-sized occupants. Its style and architecture, however, are standard Human design. It is a well-built, sturdy-looking peasant home, made of simple wood frame construction and a surprisingly sophisticated tin roof. Someone has clearly gone to some trouble to build this home, as materials for the roof would have to have been brought in at great expense from a skilled metal smith.\n\nIt is neatly tended and brightly painted in blue with white trim. The front is punctuated by a large door and two windows. The shutters on the windows are flung wide to allow the fresh air in and the smell of baking out. Like most homes in this part of the world, the windows do not have glass in them, but are covered inside by colorful curtains.\n\nTo either side of the front door of the cottage, inside a neat wooden fence, are two raised flowerbeds, well tended and weed-free. The beds are covered in soft, wood-chip\n\nmulch and the heavy clay soil sprouts colorful displays of violet delphiniums, yellow daylilies, and lavender hostas. On the east side of the house, another bed contains a variety of herbs and medicinal plants. Use the table below to determine the plants and their reputed properties. Note that these are merely the properties people believe them to have. Game Masters should determine what use, if any, a skilled herbalist could make of these plants in game terms.\n\n(Boxed Text)\n\n## Name\tUsage\tFolklore Property\n\n01 Marigold\tFresh Flowers\tComprehend language of birds 02 Columbine\tFresh Flowers\tCourage\n\n1. Blackberry\tFresh Leaves\tHealing\n1. Bay\tDried Leaves\tRemoves hexes\n1. CloverDried 4-Leaf Clovers\tSee Invisibility creatures 06 Lemon Balm Fresh Leaves\tLove\n1. Rose\tRose Hips\tGood luck\n1. Chamomile\tFresh Flowers\t\tLuck with money 09 Garlic Fresh/Dried Bulb\tProtection from vampires 10 Dill\tSeeds\t\tProtects children\n1. Mugwort\tFresh/Dried Leaves Protection from poison\n1. Raspberry\tWood\tProtection from spirits\n1. Dandelion\tHead\tTelepathy\n1. Thyme\tFresh Leaves\tRepel negative energy\n1. Celery Seeds\tSleep\n1. Geranium\tFresh Flower\tProtection from snakes\n1. Saffron\tDried Flower\tControl Gales\n1. Rue\tFresh Sprig\tProtection vs were-creatures\n1. Sage\tFresh Leaves\tGrants Wishes\n1. Amaranth\tFresh Leaves\tInvisibility (End boxed text)\n\n## Cottage Interior\n\n1. **Entryway**. Inside the cottage, visitors will find a neat living space, with sparse but stylish furnishings. Naturally, all of the furniture is also giant sized. Upon entering, visitors are greeted by a cheerfully lit scene as light pours in through the four windows. The colorfully sewn curtains are pulled back and restrained by small knit ropes to allow\n\nthe light and air to enter. In front of the door, a rectangular rug, apparently Elvish in make, greets visitors.\n\n1. **Kitchen.** The kitchen area is tidy but obviously much used. Knives and other utensils are hung from hooks beside the hearth and the cooking fireplace. A counter along the south wall holds jars and bottles and boxes filled with spices, roots, vegetables, and other food stuffs. A loaf of bread, apparently freshly baked, sits on a wooden cutting board next to a slab of butter. An amphora of cold, clear water rests to one side of the kitchen table and a keg of decent Halfling cider stands on the other.\n\nThe table is apparently where most of the food preparation takes place, and it appears that the homeowner was in the midst of brewing a pot of herbal tea when the party arrived. A cast iron kettle rests on a flat stone tile, still very hot from the fire. A teapot stands ready to receive the hot water, and a jar of dried Lemon Balm leaves is open beside it.\n\n1. **Eating Area.** To the east of the door, an enormous table and four chairs occupy the corner. The table stands some seven feet tall and the chairs are similarly massive. On top of the table rests a leather pouch containing pipeweed as well as a tankard of cider.\n\n1. **Study.** In the northeast corner of the room, a utilitarian desk is cluttered with books, scrolls, papers, and jars of ink. A cursory inspection of the books will reveal that most of the works relate to historical dissertations on an ancient tribe of hunter- gatherers who once inhabited the local area. Closer inspection will reveal many passages apparently highlighted by the reader, dealing with the shamanistic spirit magic of these peoples. Finally, a sustained study of all the works and the highlighted passages will reveal that the reader was particularly interested in burial rites and related curses. The materials might prove valuable if the collection were taken to a large city where sages or loremasters might have an interest in their historical value. Also on the desk, hidden by the clutter, is a large key which opens the chest described in area 5.\n\n1. **Chest.** Between the desk and the bed is a very large wooden chest. It is securely locked and will require a skilled hand to open without the key. Inside are a variety of Troll-sized items of clothing, as well as some older, much smaller personal items. Someone schooled in matters related to clothing or materials might realize that these items are of gnomish make. A moneybox lies at the bottom of the chest, beneath all of the clothes and other personal items. It contains a variety of coins and other valuable items collected from travelers. Random coins from many different nations add up to\n\napproximately $20000 in various denominations. A pearl necklace worth at least $3000 and several gold rings set with various stones, each valued at $1000, complete the collection.\n\n1. **Sleeping Area.** A large bed, some twelve feet long, lies behind a curtain divider. The bed is neatly made, its two pillows freshly plumped and fluffed, with the comforter turned back at one corner. The mattress is a simple one stuffed with straw, but is comfortable and warm.\n\n## Arturus the Troll\n\nThe cottage belongs to Arturus the Troll, but things are not quite what they seem. Arturus started life as a Gnome, and was an eager though inexperienced young thief when he made the mistake of seeking to pilfer the burial treasures of a tribal shaman’s tomb not far from the bridge. In centuries past, a nomadic tribe of animistic barbarians lived in these lands, and one of their most powerful shamans was put to rest in an elaborate cave tomb, well protected by magic and spirits.\n\nArturus’ attempt to break into the tomb triggered several magical traps and cost his companions their lives. Arturus escaped with his life, but suffered the effects of a powerful curse. Over the course of six painful days, he slowly transformed into a hideous Troll. When the metamorphosis was complete, he was surprised to find his mind intact. Though physically a Troll, he retains his uniquely gnomish personality.\n\nFor the past twelve years, Arturus has lived beside the bridge and amassed wealth by charging travelers for the privilege of crossing “his” bridge. When travelers arrive, he will come out of the house and greet them politely, welcoming them to his home. He will chat amicably before getting around to mentioning the toll. Arturus has no set toll. He asks travelers to donate what they think is “fair”. He will become angry if clearly offered less than the party can actually afford. He will make this judgment based upon the party’s manner and appearance. (i.e. He will be suspicious of an offer of a few copper pennies from anyone riding an expensive Horse or wearing fine clothes). In general, he expects every traveler to turn over coins or items of considerable value.\n\nArturus is heroically greedy, but despite his fearsome appearance and powerful abilities, still a noticeably cowardly little Gnome at heart. He will reason with travelers, pointing out that he maintains the bridge and keeps the area free of dangerous monsters, and that it is only fair that he be compensated. If that fails he will threaten and cajole and pose, but if confronted with combat he use his magic ring to turn\n\nInvisibility and retreat. He will not go far, however, for he has not built his comfortable little homestead solely on the gold of those too timid to challenge him. Although Arturus prefers to deal with his “customers” in a peaceful and businesslike fashion, if crossed he is quite willing to use the magic of the bridge to waylay those who seek to cheat him.\n\nWhen the bridge was built, the river saw a significant amount of boat traffic and the wizard worked with the dwarven builders to construct a very special kind of bridge which could accommodate the both land and river traffic. When the command word is spoken, the center 40-foot section of the bridge will vanish instantly, allowing tall boats to pass. This has the added benefit of dropping anyone standing on it into the churning river below. On more than one occasion, Arturus has taken his fee from the drowned body of a traveler. Anyone on the span when it vanishes gets one try to leap to safety or to grab the closest edge of the bridge before they fall into the water. (Reflex Save DC 18/Disaster Avoidance 3X Speed)\n\nShould travelers engage him in conversation and show an interest in his apparently non-Troll-like nature, he will invite them in and spend some time visiting with them. He will provide a good, hearty meal and after a few drinks may tell them his story if they appear appropriately sympathetic. Arturus has never stopped seeking a cure to his curse, and will offer the party his collected treasure, including his magic ring, should anyone be able to help break the curse. (Note: This should not be a simple matter of casting a spell on him. One possible way to help Arturus would be for the party seek out the Shaman’s tomb and explore it fully. Once the undead spirit of the Shaman is defeated, the curse would be lifted.)\n\nShould the party offer up sufficient treasure to buy passage, Arturus wishes them well and assures them that the toll is good for the return trip. He only collects from traveler heading in one direction. He does not admit that this is because so few ever return from the lands across the river…\n\n## \n\n### Reforged C&C Stats",

      "rawMarkdown": "### 1. Gulliver Dornal\nGulliver Dornal, Male Human Exp9: CR 8; Medium Humanoid ; hp 35; Fort +4, Ref +2, Will +7;\n\n## STR 16, DEX 9, CON 13, INT 12, WIS 13, CHA 11.\n\nSkills: Appraise +10, Craft (Blacksmithing) +11, Craft (Carpentry) +8, Craft (Leatherworking) +6, Craft (Locksmithing) +10.\n\n## Trading Post\n\n### Role in the Campaign\n\nIn most fantasy campaigns, much of the adventure takes places beyond the borders of the so-called civilized lands. While adventures do occur in more urban settings, the traditional quests for lost tombs and lairs of vile beasts still tend to be set in wilder, less settled areas.\n\nIn many cases, the remoteness of the location will pose something of a problem to adventurers in search of supplies. Small homesteads or mining camps will rarely have the kind of gear sought after by professional adventurers, and more importantly will not be interested in purchasing or trading for the various trinkets and baubles that adventurers might haul out of the depths of some dank tomb. Into this void comes the trading post.\n\nMuch like the general store in a larger urban setting, the trading post is a multi- purpose business. Often these businesses are part store, part tavern, part post-office, and part community center. For those hardy souls who spend their lives on the frontier, a trip to the trading post is often a much anticipated break from the routine of their lives. Generations of locals likely have met weekly at the local post, exchanged news, griped about the weather, or taxes, or marauding trolls, and sneered at itinerant adventurers.\n\nWhen adventurers first arrive in a new rural locale, it behooves them to seek out a reliable source for equipment, and trading posts are generally good places to obtain hard to find items. Chances are, if the post doesn’t have a mundane bit of adventuring gear, it can get it – though delivery of the item may take time.\n\nThe hardy souls who set off to open trading posts in the more remote corners of the world are not shy, diffident storekeepers. They are often former adventurers themselves who enjoy the steady contact with members of their former profession. Regardless of their past experience, they are almost invariably tough individualists who are willing and capable of defending their small business. Given the nature of most campaign worlds, trading posts will tend to be easily defensible, fortified places.\n\n## Variations on the theme\n\nContrary to the norm, a naïve, sickly-looking young man and his beautiful young bride run the trading post the party has arrived at. They have come to the frontier in search of a new life and haven’t the slightest idea of the dangers they face. They are still unpacking their wagon when the party first arrives, and honorable adventurers will be hard pressed to leave these newcomers to their obvious fate…\n\nThe party may stumble upon a trading post which offers bounties on the heads of various local nuisance humanoids or monsters. Goblins, orcs, trolls, and similar creatures are good candidates for bounties. The party may view this as “free” money, since they are likely to be routinely dispatching such foes anyway, but if the adventurers just happen to be at the trading post when the local monsters decide its time for some\n\npayback, a nasty battle could develop.\n\nTrading posts needn’t deal solely in the mundane. A wizard might well set up a trading post in a region where particularly rare or valuable magical components might be found, and do a brisk business trading mundane items and equipment for gems, herbs, flowers, insects, body parts, or other things with arcane potential.\n\n## Toll Road/Bridge\n\n## NOTE: The floorplan for this locale was done at a scale of 1 square = 10 feet – different than all the others!\n\n## Role in the Campaign\n\nThose who travel the roads and rivers of most fantasy worlds can readily attest to the truth of the old saying the nothing in this life is free. In particular, the use of roads and byways is rarely without costs. Whether those costs need be paid in coin or blood is not always clear.\n\nIn most cases those demanding tolls for the use of roads, bridges and fords, will be representatives of the legitimate ruler of the region. After all, it costs money to build, maintain, and patrol the roads, and surely those costs ought to be borne by those who benefit from the infrastructure. These tolls are rarely prohibitive as most local authorities have learned that given enough financial incentive, merchants and other travelers will find other ways to get to their destination. The trick is finding a toll that enriches the toll-taker without being inconvenient enough to drive business away.\n\nWhile individual tolls might not prove too much of a burden, in particularly populated areas they can become a nuisance. Areas in which control of the lands is particularly fragmented or subinfeudated may result in travelers being stopped every few miles to pay another toll. The financial costs will be unlikely to seriously inconvenience any but the most impoverished adventuring party, but heroes in a hurry may find the delays on busy roads to be maddening.\n\nIn more remote areas, away from any lawful force that might frown upon the\n\npractice, tolls may be collected by anyone with the arm strength to enforce them. Whether this be a band of woodland merry men or a powerful individual or monster, these tolls are often more painful than the legitimate type and are generally indistinguishable from outright theft.\n\nDMs should be creative in thinking about tolls. Not all treasures sought by the toll taker are monetary. A particularly nasty undead creature might haunt a river ford where it drowned and demand to drain some lifeforce (or even an entire life) in exchange for passage. A mysterious knight might insist on a test of arms before anyone can cross the bridge. A leprechaun might expect an answer to a riddle.\n\n## Variations on the theme\n\nAn adventuring party on a particularly time sensitive quest may find an encounter with a particularly officious toll taker to be infuriating. Make sure the small, bumbling bureaucrat in charge of the station is backed up by the full weight of the local authorities (making it less likely that more chaotic characters will simply hack their way through). Invent any number of regulations that require special tolls or paperwork to drag out the encounter. “Oh, you’re a Half-Orc. Let me see, I think that requires Form H8… Yes, here it is… Oh my, there’s a different algorithmic table of tolls for Half-Orcs. Let me get my abacus…” To add insult to injury, insist in payment in an obscure local currency – exact change only.\n\nCharacters arriving at a toll station discover the station manager and all his attendants dead. As they are investigating the scene, a strong force of the King’s cavalry arrives and takes them for murdering bandits…\n\nA monastery of spiritually pure, but obnoxiously self-righteous monks have established a toll booth of sorts across a mountain pass that the party simply must get through. Not interested in monetary tolls, the monks insist that anyone passing through must agree to perform a service “for the good of all”. Creative parties might think up relatively impressive sounding, but not very taxing, services.\n\n## The Troll Bridge\n\n(Text to be read to players)\n\n_As the road winds towards the river, you can clearly see ahead of you a sturdy, three-span stone bridge. The water is high and running fast, no doubt from the recent rains, as the omnipresent dark clouds serve to remind you. A giant-sized cottage stands beside the bridge, smoke curling lazily from the chimney. In front of the house, a tidy, tended garden plot shows signs of careful attention. A faint whiff of baking bread stirs your senses, perhaps aided by the memory of the depressing number of travel rations you’ve recently consumed._\n\n_The bridge appears at first glance to be just like any other stone bridge you have seen recently; perhaps a little old and run-down, but apparently structurally sound and sturdy. What is different, at least for a bridge this far away from a town or even a village, is the large cottage standing at the near end of the bridge. Other than its unusual size – the door is some 10 feet tall_\n\n_-- It would not be out of place in a quiet country thorp, or outside the walls of a baronial manor, but here, unprotected by liege or law, it defies sense that such an unfortified structure should survive the depredations of predators._\n\n_At the side of the road a crudely lettered sign has been affixed to a post, sagging to one side as it dangles from the single nail: Troll Bridge._\n\n(End players’ text)\n\n## Overview\n\nBeyond the frontiers of the civilized world, in the wilderness where there is no law save what one can assert by force of arms, many are the creatures and forces that find novel ways to amass wealth. Some will naturally seek to enrich themselves through outright theft and/or violence, but some find other ways to part travelers from their coin, albeit often with a thinly veiled threat of that same violence. If nobles and merchants can turn bridges into tollbooths, why should not a troll?\n\nAs the characters approach the troll bridge, they will be confronted by a very odd troll who will seek to charge them a toll to cross his bridge. The troll is quite powerful, but has a strong distaste for physical confrontation. Although he will fight if cornered, he prefers to attempt to reason with travelers and, if necessary, will allow them to cross the bridge (at least part way). The center of the bridge is trapped, and the unwary could well find themselves bobbing in the river. Retrieving and looting drowned corpses is still easier than fighting to this troll’s way of thinking.\n\nThe party has arrived at the only bridge for many miles across a deep, fast-running\n\nriver. Arturus, an unusual troll, has claimed the bridge and makes a comfortable living exacting tolls from passers-by.\n\nThe bridge crosses a wide expanse of water, its three stone spans bearing the weight of the 250-foot long bridge. It is wide enough for one fully loaded wagon and sturdy and strong despite it looking a bit aged. It was built more than 150 years ago by dwarves, working on commission for a mage, the ruins of whose tower can be found about a mile down the road on the other side of the bridge. As most things built by and for wizards, the bridge has its own magical secret (see description of Arturus the Troll below).\n\nIt is built of mixed field-stones, and held together by marvelous dwarven engineering with nary a drop of mortar. It has clearly seen much use over the years as its smooth surface shows the ruts of much cart and wagon traffic. The roadway over the bridge is flanked on either side by a low stone wall, approximately three feet high, to prevent the careless or the inebriated from plunging unexpectedly into the water.\n\nThe river is currently up and running high due to recent rains, and there is a barely a five foot gap between the rushing current and the bottom of the bridge. The water roars angrily between the spans, swirling madly before calming once past the structure. The water is stirred up and murky, with much debris and not a few small tree trucks bobbing past the bridge.\n\n## Cottage Exterior\n\nThe cottage is clearly built for giant-sized occupants. Its style and architecture, however, are standard human design. It is a well-built, sturdy-looking peasant home, made of simple wood frame construction and a surprisingly sophisticated tin roof. Someone has clearly gone to some trouble to build this home, as materials for the roof would have to have been brought in at great expense from a skilled metal smith.\n\nIt is neatly tended and brightly painted in blue with white trim. The front is punctuated by a large door and two windows. The shutters on the windows are flung wide to allow the fresh air in and the smell of baking out. Like most homes in this part of the world, the windows do not have glass in them, but are covered inside by colorful curtains.\n\nTo either side of the front door of the cottage, inside a neat wooden fence, are two raised flowerbeds, well tended and weed-free. The beds are covered in soft, wood-chip\n\nmulch and the heavy clay soil sprouts colorful displays of violet delphiniums, yellow daylilies, and lavender hostas. Game Masters should determine what use, if any, a skilled herbalist could make of these plants in game terms.\n\n(Boxed Text)\n\n## Name\tUsage\tFolklore Property\n\n01 Marigold\tFresh Flowers\tComprehend language of birds 02 Columbine\tFresh Flowers\tCourage\n\n1.       "rawMarkdown": "### 2. Arturus\n**Arturus**: male troll (Giant 6/Rogue 2), HP 93; AC 18; lawful evil; Primary attributes: Strength, Constitution, Dexterity; Significant attributes: Strength 23, Constitution 23, Dexterity 14, Intelligence 12, Wisdom 14, Charisma 10; Natural attacks: two claws (1d6+6) and a bite (1d6+3); Equipment: _bag of holding_ (Bag 1 – 250 pounds), _bracers of armor +2_, _ring of invisibility_ (grants invisibility at will).\n\n## Audience Chamber\n\n### Role in the Campaign\n\nWhere one finds powerful men and women, one will find those with less power vying for their attention and favors. Whether the power in question belongs to a King, a lesser noble, a merchant prince, a powerful mage, a jealous godling, or a ruthless cutthroat, almost all of these will have a room or hall in which to meet and lord over their supplicants. The audience chamber is a place where many adventuring parties will find themselves, seeking either work, reward, or mercy.\n\nIt is often the custom for local authority figures to set aside a regular block of time, be it an hour or a day each week, to hear petitions from those subject to their power. Such audiences can range from very formal appearances before a court to simple meetings between the liege and the underling. In many cases, a special room will be set aside to hear petitions.\n\nAudience chambers are often a reflection of the power that holds them. They can be austere, serious places in which the quiet dignity of the power hosting the audience dominates the room. They can be extravagant, seeking to overwhelm petitioners with awe and majesty as they gape at the gaudy display of wealth and power. In some cases, usually associated with extralegal power figures, they can be dark and hidden. The local assassins guildmaster is unlikely to greet petitioners in a rose garden, although just such a setting might put the unwary off their guard…\n\nAudience chambers belonging to the local ruler or legitimate powers tend to be more formal and are usually very busy locales, with lines of potential petitioners gathering early in the morning in the hopes of having their request heard. The person hearing the petitions is invariably surrounded by advisors, guards, servants, and other members of the household, ensuring that the rabble have no chance to harm or otherwise threaten him.\n\n## Variations on the theme\n\nIn some Kingdoms, the right to petition must be won. Each month, a tournament will be held in which the winners of several different events will be given the opportunity to petition the Queen. Some events might be martial – jousting, archery, or grand melee – while some might be more artistic – poetry, singing, or tale telling – or even mundane – plowing or ale brewing. Whatever the make up of the contests, some desperate petitioners might seek to hire professionals to compete on their behalf, hoping to have their petition carried forward.\n\nAnother possible variation is the religious audience, in which members of the faith are encouraged to come forward during one of the local holy days to seek counsel or aid from the clergy. The only catch is that the petition must be made in front of the entire congregation, and it must be the will of the gathered worshippers that the petition be granted.\n\nSome authority figures will insist on payment for any services rendered to a petitioner. Perhaps in exchange for the use of one of the manorial oxen, a peasant might be expected to work an extra week on the Lord’s fields. Or an adventuring party, petitioning for access to the Duke’s library where a crucial map is believe to be, might be asked to first find out exactly what has been eating people in the depths of the local wood.\n\n## Sample: Underworld Audience Chamber\n\nThis audience chamber belongs to a petty urban crime lord, but could easily be adapted to any other powerful figure such as a feudal nobleman or religious leader. The room serves as a place for petitioners to meet with the leader and seek favors.\n\n((text to be read to players))\n\n_The room before you is long and dim. A single bright light shines into your eyes from the far end of the room making it impossible to truly see who or what is waiting for you. As you stand conspicuously in the middle of the room, blinking into the light, you can sense your host already_\n\n_sizing you up and taking your measure._\n\n((end of player text))\n\n## Overview\n\nJust as there are different types of nobles, each with their own domains and varying degrees of power, so too does the underworld of the urban center have its own division of power. The aristocracy of crime is no less varied and no less jealous of its prerogative than its noble counterpart. Those seeking a favor unlikely to be granted by any law- abiding authority often find their way to these criminal lords and make obeisance to them just as sincerely as their true liege lord. Just such a need for extra-legal assistance might well bring characters into the audience chamber of Slink, leader of a small but sophisticated urban gang.\n\nSlink takes his role as self-appointed overseer of his domain seriously, and has long recognized the value in being seen to “give back” to the community. He regularly sets aside time for common folk to petition him for assistance, usually in response to some injustice done to them by a merchant or noble. Although it is common knowledge that these audiences take place, it is difficult, if not impossible to find anyone who will admit to ever having sought one. Word on the street is that petitioners make themselves known at one of a number of taverns run by Slink’s partners, and then wait for word on where and when to present themselves. This summons usually leads them to a remote or obscure location where they are then blindfolded and taken to one of Slink’s hideouts, where his audience chamber awaits.\n\n## Interior\n\nVisitors are led, still blindfolded, down a narrow set of stairs to a solid wooden door. They are led into a small antechamber where their blindfolds are removed and where they wait with their guide until summoned into the audience chamber. The room is sparsely furnished and dimly lit by large candelabras in each corner. Six wooden chairs are scattered around the room for those unwilling to stand.\n\nThe guide who brought them to the room is known as Archie Five-Fingers, after his favorite type of merchant’s discount. A petty thief, he has the redeeming feature of being unerringly loyal to Slink ever since “the boss” got him out of a jam with a local wizard. Archie isn’t very bright, but his orders are simple. He is to bring visitors to the antechamber and keep them there until the inner door is opened to admit the petitioners. He takes this job very seriously and will not allow visitors to leave until after they have seen Slink. Anyone trying to leave before the audience will be\n\nphysically prevented from leaving and if necessary Archie will yell for help from a waiting squad of goons at the top of the stairs.\n\nArchie is a suspicious sort, but he has a soft spot for women and priests, and will slowly open up should one of these groups appear sympathetic and interested in him. Under no circumstances however will he betray Slink.\n\nWhen Slink and his lieutenants are ready to receive the party, the inner door will open and another member of Slink’s gang will beckon to the party to enter. Archie will remain in the antechamber. Looking through the doorway into the next room, it will be apparent that the audience chamber is poorly lit except for two bright light sources behind a raised dias. The result is that it is impossible to see with any detail who or what is seated on the dias. The fact that someone is there will be evident from the voice which will call out to the visitors, “Enter and speak. My time is valuable”.\n\nThe room is rectangular and lit by candles in wall sconces. Squinting into the bright light will allow the visitor to make out what appears to be several people seated on the dias. It is impossible to make out any details of these mysterious figures or to recognize any of their features.\n\nThe room is clearly furnished to make an impression. Despite the dim light, it is easy to see that the contents of the room are of high quality and very valuable. Side tables, comfortable chairs, fine art, and rows of finely bound books line both sides of the room. The contents of the room tend to change with time, as various stolen goods are stored here until an appropriate buyer can be found.\n\nVisitors will be led forward to stand before the dias which is raised some four feet off of the ground. Looking up into the light, it will remain impossible to make out any details of the group on the dias.\n\nIn fact, Slink is accompanied by two close confidants, Norbin and Fatty Nolan. This triumvirate makes most of the important decisions regarding the status of the gang’s turf, though Slink always has the last word. Norbin is a large man whose size belies his quick wit. Fatty, on the other hand, is a gnome of reputed magical ability and prodigious appetite. Slink sits to the extreme left of the group, with Norbin sitting in the middle. Slink never speaks during audiences, leaving it to Fatty to communicate the leader’s will. After hearing a petition they will briefly confer as to whether to agree to the request and what the cost of assistance might be.\n\n## Petitioning for help\n\nOnce inside the audience chamber, visitors are expected to speak their piece quickly. Slink is a busy man and has no time to listen to long-winded tales of woe. Most likely, he has heard them before. Any tendency to wander off topic or to explain the background to a petition will result in an impatient interruption urging the petitioner to get to the point. Fatty, the spokesman for the group, has a high raspy voice that becomes higher as he becomes more annoyed.\n\nMost simple pleas for help will be granted if within the power of Slink and his gang. If the petitioner is a local resident of limited means, the request will most likely be fulfilled without any particular price attached, beyond a reminder that the petitioner owes Slink a favor.\n\nThose of greater means, merchants and the like, or those requesting slightly larger favors, will find themselves surrendering a percentage of their business, or at the very least a hefty sum of money.\n\nAnyone seeking a particularly difficult or dangerous service – breaking a pal out of the city gaol for example – will be required to agree to perform a major service for Slink.\n\nSlink and his partners are prepared to consider almost any request. They are strictly businessmen in this matter, and have no moral qualms about contracting to kill, kidnap, or steal, though obviously the cost to the petitioner is considerably higher for these more nefarious deeds.\n\nThe following is a list of examples of small, large, and “special” favors, as well as some suggested services to be performed for special favors.\n\n## Small favors\n\nHelp to recover a debt Help pay taxes\n\nHelp to get a job\n\nHelp get medical attention\n\n## Large favors\n\nHave someone killed\n\nHave something valuable stolen\n\nDefy or oppose the will of a nobleman or rich merchant Retrieve loved one (either kidnapped or willingly departed)\n\nDiscredit rival\n\nFrame someone for a crime\n\nSeek protection from a rival gang\n\n## Special Favors\n\nDefy the sovereign\n\nRescue someone from royal dungeon Kill a powerful figure\n\nOppose a Temple or other religious institution Oppose a wizard\n\n## Quests for Slink\n\nRetrieve a particular magical item from the city vaults. This item was stolen by Slink’s gang, but recovered by the authorities during the arrest of several of the perpetrators.\n\nEmbarrass and humiliate a rival gang leader by kidnapping a relative.\n\nKill a particularly troublesome law enforcement figure but make it look like an accident.\n\nEscort someone to a distant city and then bring them back safely.\n\nReplace a valuable object with a valueless duplicate and return with the original.\n\n## \n\nFILENAME \\p C:\\Documents and Settings\\John\\My Documents\\Roleplaying Games\\Backup GFW Essential Places Jan 17\\Awaiting Game Info v12\\Underworld Audience Chamber v1.2.doc\n\n## Wizard’s Tower\n\n### Role in the Campaign\n\nWhat wilderness would be complete without a lonely stone tower housing a mad wizard and his arcane experiments? What city lacks an imposing tower belonging to a powerful spell-caster, famous for her knowledge of local denizens and phenomena? Since RPGs have been around, it has been natural to associate towers and wizards. These places offer up boundless opportunities for adventure, housing either a patron, a mentor, an advisor, or a foe.\n\nUsually built to ensure security and privacy, the average wizard’s tower (if one could be so bold as to speak of an average wizard) is built of stone and raised via magical means. It is designed to deter unwanted visitors, to prevent prying eyes, and to provide a quiet and structurally sturdy locale for experiments into new and dangerous magics.\n\nMany wizards will build their towers in remote locations, and even those who choose to live in built-up areas will often locate their towers on the outskirts of settlements. As mentioned, wizards tend to value their privacy and security. Some civic minded mages also keep in mind the potential devastation that might be caused by an experiment gone wrong, and therefore keep their abode at a distance from innocent victims.\n\nWizardly towers tend to be dangerous places to attempt to penetrate. Aside for the\n\nnatural danger resident in the homeowner, these locales tend to be protected by a variety of guards and wards of an arcane nature. Rooftop gargoyles may animate, fearsome constructs may patrol the halls, and the building itself may turn against intruders, with shifting walls and magically locked doors. Some towers lack even a conventional entrance, with ingress and egress depending upon the magical ability to translocate.\n\nDepending upon the nature of the campaign, wizards may play a central role in local government. In a magocracy, the local Lord will doubtless be a wizard, ruling the immediate area from his tower. In more mundane forms of government, some wizards may still be recognized as temporal Lords, depending upon their history of service to the crown. If not the local authority themselves, wizards often serve as advisors and defenders of\n\nDepending upon the nature of the campaign, wizards may play a central role in local government. In a magocracy, the local Lord will doubtless be a wizard, ruling the immediate area from his tower. In more mundane forms of government, some wizards may still be recognized as temporal Lords, depending upon their history of service to the crown. If not the local authority themselves, wizards often serve as advisors and defenders of the local nobility. This depends very much on the personality of the wizards, as some prefer to be left alone to pursue their own agendas.\n\n## Variations on the Theme\n\nA particularly paranoid wizard might build a tower that is completely without windows or doors. The entire building might appear to be one seamless piece of stone or metal, defying anyone to gain entrance. Discussions with the locals will reveal that no one has ever seen anyone enter or leave the tower, but the wizard does simply show up in town sometimes… Is there a regular entrance hidden by illusions? Does the tower require some sort of magical entrance key? Or is there simply a hidden entrance somewhere (of somewhen?) else?\n\nPowerful wizards may make their homes in various locations. One possibility for a wizards tower would be a multidimensional building in which each room actually existed in a different dimension; with doorways simply functioning as portals between them. Entering or leaving such a tower could have unexpected consequences as visitors find themselves deposited in unlikely places.\n\nSimilarly, a wizard’s tower might well move through time and space. Perhaps the entire tower moves via teleportation either at its master’s whim or in relation to an\n\nexternal phenomena, like the phase of the moon. If an adventuring party is in need of assistance from a Wizard who lives in such a tower, their first quest might well be to figure out the pattern of movement of the tower and arrange to be in an appropriate location when it arrives!\n\n## Sample: The Peculiar Tower of Petronious Prime\n\n((Text to be read to players))\n\nWhen bards gather to sing of the great mages, or when epic tales are told of wizards bold and grim, the name of Petronious Prime never comes up. However, should the conversation ever turn to wizards with particularly bizarre personalities, Petronious proud takes his place of honor.\n\nBefore you now, rising some five stories tall, lies the peculiar tower of Petronious Prime, an edifice of such renown that even the hardened adventurers among you cannot completely suppress a jolt of excitement. You are about to meet a legend.\n\n((end player text))\n\n## Overview\n\nPetronious Prime is a wizard of some minor fame, less for his impressive contributions to the study of the arcance than for the bizarre magical tower in which he lives. The tower appears normal, if gaudy, from the exterior, but is anything but once visitors arrive within.\n\nPetronious is now approaching 120 years of age and has spent almost his entire life studying what he describes as the magic of chaos. He has striven to harness unpredictable forces and make them predictable. He has delved deep into the mysteries of translocation magic and the links between the location of objects and their inherent magical energy. His life’s work is embodied in his tower, which to him serves as an almost living extension of his will, but for others serves as a sort of randomized series of unconnected places and things.\n\nFamously irritable, Petronious receives few visitors. Gaining entry to his abode will not prove simple, but it can be achieved if visitors can convince his gatekeeper, a minor construct that Petronious joking calls a “chaos golem”, that their petition will be of interest to the mage.\n\nWhat is the secret to Petronious’ famous tower? The contents of the tower randomly rearrange themselves at unpredictable intervals. This includes any visitors and their\n\npossessions. Petronious appears able to exercise some control over this phenomena, but no one is sure how the transformations occur or how Petronious molds them to his will.\n\nA typical transformation happens without warning. One moment a visitor might be sitting in a comfortable armchair on the third floor, and the next find himself seated on a potato sack in the cellar. The transformations seem to happen without rhyme or reason – room contents do not move together and sometimes pieces of furniture disappear completely, only to reappear at some random time in the future, likely in another room. During these transformations, the rooms themselves seem to move within the tower. One might be in a library, gazing out a ground floor window at one moment, and suddenly find oneself in a kitchen on the fifth floor.\n\nOnly Petronious is capable of interacting with the tower in a structured way. Somehow, the tower exercises a sort of prescience, knowing what Petronious wants or needs and ensures that the appropriate items are handy regardless of the apparent contents of the room. Thus, should Pertronious suddenly desire an apple from the pantry, he might open a drawer on a nearby desk, rummage briefly through the assorted papers and implements within, and then withdraw a fresh, juicy apple, still cool from the cellar.\n\nThis mysterious link between Petronious and the tower surprises and awes most visitors. When Petronious is ready to sleep, visitors suddenly realize that his bed is in the room. Should he desire to leave the tower, the front door is in the wall in front of him, even if moments before he was on the top floor. The tower reacts to Petronious’ whims as if it were sentient, but it is important to note that at no time will Petronious ever speak of the tower in this way, or act as if it were anything other than a normal house. He does not speak to the building (“Tower, get me some beer”), he merely wants a beer and the tower makes one available.\n\nFor anyone other than Petronious, the experience of his tower usually starts out as amusing, but often turns frustrating or even terrifying. Tales tell of one particular visitor, a distant and unpopular relative of Petronious, who spent a month seeking an exit. The wise man always looks to see what is on the opposite side of any door in the tower before passing through.\n\n## Tower Exterior\n\nThe tower of Petronious Prime looks to be five stories tall, with an open roof-top garden. The walls are made of slick black stone of a variety unknown to any geologists in the party. The walls appear seamless, giving the appearance that the entire building\n\nis carved from solid rock, and the only clue to its bizarre nature is the way in which windows randomly appear and disappear around the tower.\n\nThe front door is a sturdy, magical portal made of the same material as the rest of the tower exterior. It can only be opened from the inside or by the will of Petronious. It swings soundlessly on unseen hinges.\n\nThe keeper of the door is Willis, a chaos golem. Chaos golems are magical constructs, and Willis serves to keep the gawking masses from pestering Petronious. Willis appears on the wall of the tower, next to the front door, as a vaguely humanoid face which extrudes from the rock. Willis’ features are different every time he appears but sometimes resemble a caricature of a previous visitor. Willis will speak with visitors and should he be convinced of their bona fides, he will allow the door to open to permit them entry. It is important to note that Willis is no more predictable than anything else in the tower, and exactly what kinds of petitions he will find worthy varies greatly. Some days he may turn away an adventuring party on a noble quest while admitting someone with a less urgent need.\n\nThe position of the front door never appears to change – at least from the outside. It is always on the southern wall of the tower and it is surrounded by pleasant flower beds.\n\n## Tower Interior\n\nHow does one describe the interior of rooms which may well change at any moment? Visitors to Petronious’ tower can count on few immutable facts, but there are a couple of things which appear to remain constant. Rooms within the tower are all round, approximately sixty feet in diameter, with a spiral stone staircase rising through the center of the room. Most rooms will have 1-3 windows, though the shape, location, and form of those windows may vary.\n\nDoors, windows, and the stairs are perilous things within the tower, and wise visitors learn to stay in one place, rather than wandering through the structure. Anytime someone passes from one room to another or through a doorway, the DM should randomly determine what is on the other side. Even though it is possible to look through a doorway and see the room on the other side, there is no guarantee that what is seen will still be there when the doorway is traversed.\n\nFor the purposes of DMs running the tower, there is a flat 10% chance per 15 mins that the contents of the rooms will randomly change. There is also an 80% chance that\n\nthe contents of the rooms will change anytime someone goes up or down a flight of stairs, or uses a door.\n\nThe transformation takes place instantly and without warning. Interestingly, the phenomenon never results in injury to people in the tower. Furniture never materializes inside living organisms or in mid-air (where it might fall on unsuspecting victims). The contents of the ever changing rooms appear in a neatly arranged fashion, not a random jumble of furnishings.\n\nRooms appear to change in a completely random fashion, but generally follow relatively logical patterns (i.e. the contents of any given room will be more or less arranged by function so that beds don’t appear at the same time as the contents of the root cellar). There also appears to be an almost infinite combination of furnishings which come and go. It is dangerous to put anything possessions down in this tower, as the table they are placed on could well vanish (with the items on it) and not return to the tower for a very long time. The exception to this is of course the fact mentioned above that Petronious can retrieve any item he desires at will due to his bond with the tower.\n\nIt is important to note that due to the random nature of the shifting of the rooms, it is quite possible to become trapped in the tower unless Petronious himself leads you to the front door. Because the contents of the rooms shift whenever the stairs are used, and because the shifts are random, there is no guarantee that going downstairs to the “ground floor” will result in finding the exit. The main door to the tower is just as likely to be found on the third floor as the first, though through another quirk in the magic of the tower exiting the main door always deposits the traveler outside on the ground and never three stories in the air. Thus it is impossible to predict where one might find the way out, or the kitchen, the bedchambers. Indeed, without the active assistance of Petronious, the tower can become something of a house of horrors. Tales tell of some visitors who eventually threw themselves out of windows to escape.\n\nAs mentioned, when the rooms transform they tend to do so in such a way that their contents are distributed logically. When a DM determines that the rooms have shifted, he should consult the following tables to determine the general function of the new room and the new location of the room within the tower.\n\n((begin tables)) Room Functions\n\nColumn 1 Column Two\n\n01 – 05 Entry hall (includes main door!) 06 – 10 Kitchen\n\n11 – 15 Bedroom\n\n16 – 20 Storage Area\n\n21 – 25 Roof-top Garden\n\n26 – 30 Magical Laboratory\n\n31 – 35 Library\n\n36 – 40 Bathroom\n\n41 – 45 Sitting Room\n\n46 – 50 Dungeon Cell\n\n51 – 55 Music Room\n\n56 – 60 Guest Quarters\n\n61 – 65 Pantry\n\n66 – 70 Salon\n\n71 – 75 Empty\n\n76 – 80 Solarium\n\n81 – 85 Study\n\n86 – 90 Dining Hall\n\n91 – 95 Great Room\n\n96 – 00 Mixed (roll twice) ((end table))\n\n((begin table)) Room Location\n\nColumn 1 Column 2\n\n01 – 02 Ground Floor\n\n03 – 04 Second Floor\n\n05 – 06 Third Floor\n\n07 – 08 Fourth Floor\n\n09 – 10 Fifth Floor\n\n((end table))\n\n## Some sample rooms\n\n### Entryway\n\n1. Doorway\n\nThe door to Petronious’ tower is surprisingly flimsy. It is neither warded by magic nor by a strong lock. The magical nature of the tower itself (not to mention his own power) is sufficient protection for Petronious. Anyone entering without the prior approval of Willis, the door warden, will find that as soon as they have passed through the doorway, the room will shift and become a dark, dank, dungeon cell without exits, and it will not shift again until Petronious wills it. Petronious usually remembers to check on prisoners regularly, but he is getting old…\n\n1. Trapdoor\n\nIn theory, this trapdoor leads down into a root cellar and general storage area. Obviously, given the nature of the tower, it is just as likely to lead to the roof, or the bathroom.\n\n1. Sitting area\n\nA small sitting area appears recently vacated. A warm cup of mulled cider still sits beside an open journal and a dagger, the tip still wet with blood. A quick scan of the journal reveals, however, that the last entry was made over fifty years ago, apparently by a young woman. A careful read of the entire journal will show that it contains nothing of interest beyond the daily musings of a self-conscious young girl. Anyone familiar with the working of the tower will quickly surmise that these items have been randomly thrown together, but newcomers may find the table’s contents quite a puzzle.\n\n1. Storage\n\nPetronious uses the space behind the stairs in the entryway as a temporary storage area. Boxes, bags, chests, and assorted containers are piled haphazardly here. Although the exact configuration of the pile, as well as the contents of the containers, changes with every shift of the room, the area always remains a cluttered storage space.\n\n1. Cupboards\n\nA couple of tall cupboards are here, one containing hooks upon which are hung various coats, cloaks, hoods, and other outdoor wear. The other contains shelves filled with boots, walking sticks, gloves and similar accoutrements.\n\n1. Stairway\n\nA stone, spiral staircase leads upwards from the entryway to the next level of the tower. All staircases in the tower are identical, and with the exception of the entry level\n\nand the roof-top garden, they all lead both up and down. The stairs are smooth, worn stone and are very treacherous if wet. Even when dry, any attempt to run up or down the stairs carries with it a significant chance of slipping and falling.\n\n## Kitchen\n\n1. Firepit\n\nAll cooking is done here, over a bed of hot coals. The fireplace has two rotisseries for roasting meat, as well as a small cauldron suspended over one side of the fire. Although no chimney is visible from the outside of the tower, from the inside the fireplace appears to connect to a flue. Where the smoke goes is something of a mystery.\n\n1. Two long tables serve as preparation space. They are generally cluttered with food in various stages of preparation, kitchen implements, spices, and other cooking essentials. Although the tables always contain at least one (and usually several) completed dishes, suitable for a simple meal, at no time does Petronious actually cook. The food seems to appear from out of nowhere, every time the room shifts. It is always warm, tasty, and fresh.\n\n1. Well\n\nDespite the fact that the kitchen moves between floors like all the other rooms, it contains a small well. Although there is no logical explanation for its presence, the well always produces cold, fresh water. Anyone diving into the well will find that it is approximately 30 feet deep, and the bottom is littered with coins in various denominations, adding up to approximately $100.\n\n1. Kitchen cupboards\n\nThese are standard cupboards containing the necessary utensils and flatware of a kitchen. The contents vary depending upon the shifting of the room with the simple pottery being replaced with fine china or silver place settings. Currently, the dishes in the cupboards are of very fine quality, with a set of crystal goblets bearing the crest of a long extinct noble family.\n\n1. Storage\n\nIt appears that the kitchen has recently been resupplies, as bags of flour and boxes of various foodstuffs have been piled here pending unpacking. Several small kegs of fine brandy are included in the jumble.\n\n## Magical Laboratory\n\nThis floor is dedicated to Petronious’ ongoing magical research. As might be expected, much of his work relates to multi-dimensional spaces and teleportation. The lab should contain at least 3 minor and 1 major magic items in a functional condition and a similar number of non-functional prototypes.\n\nSummoning circle\n\nAt one time, Petronious’ research focused on the summoning of extra-dimensional beings. This graven circle of protection was a part of those experiments and served him well in numerous summoning rites. Although he no longer dabbles in such matters, the circle remains functional and requires only the appropriate rituals and invocations to be reactivated.\n\n1. Bookcases\n\nPetronious has traveled widely throughout multiverse, and collected obscure tomes and texts related to things magical. At any given time, there are between 50 and 70 books of lore on these shelves. Most are written in obscure, dead languages, often from other dimensions or planes. Careful study, usually with magical assistance to decipher the arcane languages will allow a wizard character to learn one previously unknown spell per month of study.\n\n1. Work Area\n\nThese tables are littered with papers, components, tools, and other paraphernalia related to the creation of magical items. Although Petronious rarely crafts items these days, the area is littered with the detritus of his previous work.\n\nA careful search of the work area will turn up 4-40 components of use in spell casting. 10% of these will be rare, exotic, or expensive components such as the congealed blood of a near extinct monster. 30% will be relatively uncommon, such as powdered gemstone, while 60% will be common components.\n\nThe tables will also contain at least 1 functional magic wand, 3 scrolls containing arcane spells, and one miscellaneous magical item. The DM should decide the exact nature of these magic items, depending of course upon the magic level of the campaign in question, but the miscellaneous magic item at least should be an exotic object, never before encountered by the adventuring party. It might well be a beneficial but perilous item, or possible a long lost treasure of renown. Keep in mind though that Petronious is not likely to part easily with any of these items.\n\n1. Strange Portal\n\nA 5-foot diameter sphere of blue light, crackling with energy, hovers about a foot off of the ground. Even the most mundane of characters will be able to sense without any effort that the sphere exudes intense magical energy.\n\nThose more attuned to the arcane will be able to sense the chaotic, turbulent flows of magic that surround the sphere. The portal itself is the heart of the tower, responsible for the extra-dimensional transport of the towers contents. A careful study of the portal – something which would require at least ten years of research – would eventually reveal that the portal exists simultaneously in over a hundred different dimensions.\n\nThe portal is, however, an extremely dangerous artifact to experiment with, as it is completely uncontrollable. Merely being in the presence of the portal causes items to randomly transport themselves between dimensions, as evidenced by the behaviour of items within the tower. Anything or anyone that actually enters the portal will be instantly transported at random to another dimension. Unfortunately, each item’s destination is determined at random, so a fully equipped adventurer entering the portal will almost certainly arrive naked. Even if one were fortunate enough to travel to the same dimension as one’s equipment though, one will discover that the actual spatial location of arrival in the new dimension is also completely random, so the traveler and his gear could still arrive in widely separated locations. It is also important to note that there is no “other end” of the portal at the destination, making returning to Petronious’ tower virtually impossible.\n\nNeedless to say, adventurers are strongly advised against entering the portal. Anyone casting detection magics on the portal will get a sense of strong chaotic magic and a sense of strong foreboding. DMs should advise players that their characters feel very uneasy about the portal, and even the most mundane of characters should sense something “wrong” about the sphere. Given these hints, anyone choosing to enter the sphere deserves their fate!\n\nIf asked, Petronious will be unable to explain the origin of the portal. If pressed about his apparently unique relationship with the chaos of the portal, such as its apparent ability to anticipate his desires and reshape items at his whim, he will speculate that the portal itself has a limited sentience. The study of the Chaos Portal in fact makes up the bulk of his life’s work.\n\n# ESSENTIAL PLACES BIBLE MATERIAL\n\nWhat is needed is a book full of locations with floor plans in varied scale as appropriate to the size of the place/levels or floors depicted, each plan showing fixtures, furniture, doors and windows, etc. With that depiction there needs be s selection of persons, several each proprietor and worker types and their general abilities, and guidelines for the numbers and sorts of other persons likely encountered in the establishment. With that information for commercial places there needs be a list of goods purveyed and/or services offered. Concluding the treatment for a location, a few brief adventure hooks.\n\nAbout the only prefatory text really needed is an introductory bit, a discussion of how to make the standard floor plans varies so as to make the same sort of place seem different in a different location, and a discussion of the monetary system employed in the work, how to adapt it to a specific game system--for the one to be used will fit in any literary work simply by using specific coin names.\n\nOn request Gary Gygax will supply electronic files from his mss. for the information in the works cited hereafter, and more details of the LA game monetary system if needed.\n\n# ESSENTIAL PLACES: LIKELY LOCATIONS\n\nAudience chamber/great hall (for placement anywhere) Barn\n\nBarracks\n\nBed chamber (inn-type, private)\n\nBed chamber (tavern-type, multiple persons) Cottage (farm house)\n\nDungeon prison\n\nFane \n\nGaol\n\nGaol (town)\n\nGuild—high and low varieties (merchants’ vs. thieves’ for example) Guard room\n\nGuard room (for placement anywhere)\n\nInn (see _Yggsburgh_ book, Green Dragon Inn and The Outs Inn) Kitchen, large (as in a palace)\n\nManor house/villa\n\nShrine \n\nTavern (see _Yggsburgh_ book)\n\nTemple \n\nThrone room\n\nTown house Warehouse\n\n#### _See also lists of locations below and select any deemed essential such as a Gemner, etc._\n\n## Special thanks:\n\nJohn Morrow for his initial work on this project.\n\nGary Gygax for the monetary system locations, and extensive lists of prices for\n\ngoods and services.\n\n## EQUIPMENT LISTS\n\n### Note on Prices and Selling\n\nThe prices listed for goods and materials represent average values. Depending on the location, rarity, or disposition of the seller, actual costs may vary—sometimes rising to double the listed amount or falling to half or less. Such adjustments are entirely at the discretion of the Game Master, reflecting local economy, scarcity, or simple opportunism.\n\nWhen selling items to a merchant or purveyor, characters can expect to receive anywhere from 20% to 70% of that merchant’s usual selling price. Thus, an item worth 100 in local currency might bring as little as 20 or as much as 70 when sold, depending on market conditions and the negotiator’s skill. As always, supply and demand in the setting dictate the outcome.\n\nShould a character establish their own place of business, prices are naturally theirs to set. Sales and trade in this case should be resolved through the Game Master’s impartial adjudication, balancing opportunity, realism, and narrative flow.\n\n### Antiquities\n\n### The sale of antiquities follows different principles, as such items often carry historical or cultural value beyond their material worth. Antiquities generally fall into three broad classes\n\n**Coins**: In smaller or isolated communities, old coins are usually treated as little more than curiosities—worth about 10% to 20% less than, or at best equal to, current currency. In more sophisticated or urban markets, however, collectors and numismatists may pay a premium. As a rough measure, small quantities of ancient coins might fetch between 200% and 600% (roll one six-sided die) of their metal value. Larger hoards, being less rare, usually earn a lesser increase—typically 120% to 220% (roll two six-sided dice).\n\n**Jewelry**: Apply the same general rules as for coins, though quantity is rarely a factor. Determine the value of any gemstones included and add their full worth to the metal value before applying the multiplier for antiquity. The craftsmanship, age, and provenance of a piece may significantly enhance its price.\n\n**Objects d’Art**: This category includes all manner of valuable artifacts—antique armor, garments, paintings, tapestries, sculpture, and other works of artistry or devotion. The worth of such items depends entirely on the world of your campaign. Use real-world analogues as a guide, adjusting for rarity and the degree of interest in such things among the people and cultures of your setting.\n\nArbitrary values are acceptable, provided they remain reasonable and do not eclipse the broader balance of the campaign—except in cases where a singular treasure serves as the central reward of a great adventure. Truly priceless items may exist, but as in all tales, _the really big one usually gets away._\n\nA treasure valued at a million in local currency is not implausible, especially if divided among a party of adventurers—but even then, fortune is fickle. Players may sell too cheaply, misjudge a relic’s worth, or fall prey to swindlers and con artists. Such moments often lead to as much storytelling delight as the adventure itself.\n\nMarkets may shift, demand may vanish, or fakes may circulate. The Game Master should use these circumstances to enrich the world and remind players that, in trade as in treasure-hunting, luck and cleverness are as valuable as gold.\n\n**_Extraordinary Items:_** Sale of Extraordinary things is also a different matter.\n\n_Memory Tablets:_ These are pretty dear, and something in the neighborhood of a\n\n$10,000 value is not outrageous. In short supply, the cost might be more than twice that.\n\nof course! Guild members will possibly receive a discount.\n\n_Powers and Like Extraordinary Ability Related Knowledge:_ If for example, your campaign assumes that any Power or the like is worth about at least $1,000 per Grade or AEP it costs to use it, then the sale of such thing to a guild will fetch about half price, to an individual whatever that one will pay. Unique ones, though, are worth at least double the price of the “known and standard” ones.\n\n_Extraordinary Items:_ These are not considered as things one is able to purchase. Their sale value to other than an Avatar is basically the sum of the price of a non- Extraordinary item of the same sort, plus from $1,000 to $10,000 for each special feature. Consider protection bonuses and striking plus harm ones at about the middle to top range and multiply per point. A long spear that adds 10 to weapon precision and 6-8 points of harm is thus worth its normal weapon base plus $72,000 to $90,000 more for its addition to success in striking and its harm. A sword surely has the $10,000 per point addition. Use common sense and base it on the way you want your campaign to run. Any supernatural bonus, 25 or more precision bonus, 17 or more harm bonus, _doubles_ the cost for such. If the long spear noted above was +25 weapon precision and added 17-20 harm. The price would be normal weapon base plus $150,000 to $200,000 doubled,\n\ni.e. $300,000 to $400,000.\n\n# ITEMS BY COMMERCIAL LOCATION, LOCATION NAME ALPHABETICAL\n\nLegend Masters might find this particularly helpful in setting up the various shops and stores in communities.
